review_comments.body:
The base 10 path looks right to me: 0 differences from V8 on 100k random decimal strings (up to 40 digits, signs, trailing junk).

The same double rounding is still here for radix 4, 8, 16 and 32, though, and for those the spec does not allow an approximation either (only a radix that is not 2, 4, 8, 10, 16 or 32 may be implementation-approximated). Examples on this branch vs node 24:

```js
parseInt("c760b46463a0c40d05", 16)  // goja 3.677870375570711e+21, V8 3.677870375570712e+21
parseInt("itaunfap8aa0q", 32)       // goja 21809762542452810000,  V8 21809762542452814000
parseInt("-1701324071575532202006324217", 8) // goja -4.540150585159297e+24, V8 -4.5401505851592977e+24
```

On 100k random strings in radix 2/4/8/16/32, 117 come out one ULP off.

One way to cover every radix with a single rounding is to let `math/big` do it (already imported elsewhere in the package):

```go
func parseLargeInt(s string, base int, sign bool) Value {
	end := 0
	for end < len(s) && digitVal(s[end]) < base {
		end++
	}
	x, _ := new(big.Int).SetString(s[:end], base)
	f, _ := new(big.Float).SetInt(x).Float64() // nearest, ties to even; +Inf on overflow
	if sign {
		f = -f
	}
	return valueFloat(f)
}
```

called as `parseLargeInt(s, base, sign)` from both overflow branches. With that, the same 100k radix 2/4/8/16/32 strings match V8 with 0 differences (base 10 stays at 0 too).

comments.body:
Thanks @bardrop, I took your suggestion: for radix 4/8/16/32 `parseInt` now goes through `math/big`, so large inputs are rounded once instead of per digit. I added a test with your three examples, compared against V8's results. `go test .` passes.

This comment was drafted with Claude Code.

Re-checked at 6c2c4bc: 20k random strings (signs, leading space, `0x`, trailing junk, up to 60 digits) against node 24 give 0 differences for radix 2, 4, 8, 10, 16 and 32. The only differences left are radix 3, 7 and 36, in the last digit, which the spec lets an implementation approximate. Looks good to me.
